designs.name: Task-claimed squads: HUNT / CONVOY / GUARD / RAID roles over a shared task table
designs.summary: Ducks claim a small number of team tasks through capped, heartbeat-counted claim slots in the shared array, so no central commander is needed. The tasks are: HUNT an enemy carrier holding our flag, using a shared track that predicts where the carrier is after it leaves view; CONVOY our own carrier, with escorts on stations and a leash, and re-grabs done by the convoy; GUARD a threatened flag, with the guard sized to the threat; and later RAID, a pre-formed convoy that goes to an enemy flag. Every other duck stays the unchanged g_iter1 field army, and Micro.fight gets the objective of a role duck (goal, leash, mode) through static fields set each turn. HUNT comes first because it targets the largest measured share of their captures: 312 of their 453 captured trips last 20 rounds or more, and long trips with fewer than 0.5 of our ducks nearby are captured 71% of the time, against 24% with 3 or more nearby. The plan has six stages, S0 to S5. S0 is plumbing and instruments with byte-identical behaviour. S1 to S2 each have execution diagnostics that separate a broken mechanism from a wrong premise, and each must pass a pre-registered paired delivery block. Only then does the S3 composite get a band test plus a paired block against the upper tier. The budget is at most 12 arms and about 4 VM days, with closing criteria written before S1.

designs.name: Situation Board: shared carrier tracks with claim-bounded interception
designs.summary: Our ducks often see the enemy carrier pick up our flag, then forget it within 5 rounds. A replay census of 232 B3 band games shows the scale. Of their 132 long (25+ rounds) unopposed captured trips, 62% had one or more of our ducks within dist2 20 at the pickup (mean 2.35). On long trips their capture rate is 74% with fewer than 0.5 chasers on average, 49% with 0.5-2 and 31% with 2 or more. The design adds a shared world model in slots 23-63, written by every duck and read by every duck. It holds enemy carrier tracks with straight-line prediction, a state machine per flag (home, carried, dropped, missing, lost, gone), a 6-sector board (allies counted exactly, enemies as a lower bound, nearest-threat distance) and a 12-entry claim table. The claim table picks the K ducks with the best interception ETA, and Micro.fight receives their goal through its existing goal parameter; every other duck plays exactly as g_iter1. The plan is staged so the sensor is proven before any consumer is built. S0a is a truth-only premise test on existing replays; S0b is the model with no behaviour change, checked for identity and scored against replay truth through indicator dots; S1 is interception, then S2 (threat routing) and S3 (convoy), each behind its own premise number. Every stage has pre-registered paired statistics against g_iter1, and the programme has a hard budget and a written closing criterion.

designs.name: Objective-Driven Micro (ODM): shared flag-trip tracks, a capped responder auction, and an objective branch in Micro.fight
designs.summary: ODM keeps every flag trip visible after the carrier leaves vision. It does this with one shared track per flag, with dead reckoning, a missing-from-home detector and continuity across drops. A capped responder auction in slots 23-44 then makes the k ducks best placed to intercept an enemy carrier (CUT) or to escort our own carrier (ESCORT) into objective holders, whether or not they are in a fight. Micro.fight takes the objective as one extra tile-scoring branch, used only by those committed ducks. Strike-first, targeting and strike/heal-after-move stay as they are, and every other duck keeps g_iter1's micro byte for byte. The design aims at the measured binding term: 106 of 151 losses are by capture, 47% of their captured trips walk home with nobody of ours near, 64% come from re-grab or relay chains, and our escorts are 4.85 against their 6.76. It meets the written re-open condition of the closed flag-pressure family (tracking with prediction plus a dedicated group). The plan is staged: S0 has no behaviour change, proves identity at k=0 and measures the premise offline on the existing 234 g_iter1 band replays. S1 (CUT) and S2 (ESCORT) each get a 5(a) signature that separates execution failure from premise failure, a delivery block with bars written now and a dose ladder on k. The budget is at most 7 mini-blocks and 3 band runs, and the closing criterion is written before any code.

designs.name: Tide: commander-timed mass waves
designs.summary: Robot idx 0 becomes a per-round commander. It reads team totals that every duck adds into the shared array (alive, massed at the rally, contact front, strike kills, deaths) and runs a MASS -> PUSH -> CONVOY cycle with one shared rally, one shared objective and a line-abreast formation. A push launches only when the army is gathered and the numbers estimate (our alive vs 50 minus our kills in the last 25 jail rounds) is not against us; it ends when its own exchange turns bad. Micro.fight keeps its strike, heal and carrier branches but now takes the order. In a push, with the wave in view, it advances at margin 1 and leans toward the objective. In MASS, stragglers and hurt ducks fall back to the mass, and respawned ducks join at the rally instead of trickling in. Economy is timed to the cycle: wave 1 sweeps the centre crumbs at r201, ducks collect crumbs in the lull, the bank goes into a stun barrage at push onset, and kills made in their half earn the +30 bounty. Six switch-gated stages follow (S0 instruments and premise screen, then S1-S5, with S6 optional). Each has a replay signature that separates execution failure (supShare, cohesion, lone and trickle deaths, the push timeline) from premise failure (upper-tier exchange by r600, ground, capture difference). Budget and closing criteria are written in advance.

scores.name: Design 3: Objective-Driven Micro (ODM): shared flag-trip tracks, capped responder auction, objective branch in Micro.fight
scores.strengths: Best match to the measured binding term, with mechanism-level reasons why each closed arm failed, and I checked those reasons against the code and the log. (1) Its critique of the rush micro is correct. In Micro.java:205, the goal term d2(goal)*4 grows with distance: one step toward a goal d tiles away is worth about 8d points, so beyond about 19 tiles it outweighs RUSH_THREAT_COST 150 and walks into threats. Its objective branch scores Chebyshev progress (±1 per step) times 300 against 250 per threat, which does not depend on distance. It also replaces engage, advance and kite only for committed ducks, so responders are not pinned by side fights. This matters because ducks see an enemy about 95% of the time. (2) Its claim that 'ESCORT_R2 = 20 is the measurement radius itself' is right. Duck.java:42 recruits only allies within dist2 20, so escorts20 could not rise; g1esc and g1escrg read flat at 4.37-5.55. (3) Tracks are keyed by flag and survive drops ('presumed re-grabbed unseen' after the window). This fits the chain evidence: I recomputed from trips-b2fs that 141 of the 453 captures last under 20 rounds and 97% of those are non-first, i.e. final legs of chains that only flag-continuity reaches. (4) Premise thresholds P1-P6 are offline and cost no bot code, on the g_iter1 band replays, which are kept (tools/keep-replays.txt lists g_iter1). They include reachInFight as the price indicator. (5) It says plainly what it does not attack (economy, territory). It uses the REWRITE_EVAL bars verbatim. The k=4/8 dose ladder directly tests the 'more bodies against the 6.76 escort pack' answer. (6) Two side claims check out: OF_HOME is missing from BotTest's slot list, and OF_ALERT is a usable estimate of pickup time.
scores.weaknesses: The delivery checks are still proxies (chasers20, enemyUnseenRounds), and captures appear only as a guard; diagnosis point 2 warns about exactly this. Conversion is tested only at the M1 band test and by the correlational P6. k is fixed and not sized to the observed escorts until the conditional S4. The binomial-thinning auction with parity double-buffering is the most complex claim mechanism of the three, so execution failure is likely; diagnostic (2) does catch it. The bytecode estimate for roundStart (120 worst) is low: clearing 6 AUC slots plus the stamp is 7 writes at 75 each, about 525. The total still fits. P2's threshold (reach ≥ 4) counts ducks that are fighting. ESC (S2) runs against the b2rgc evidence that our carriers die within about 3 moves inside their spawn; it is gated by P4 and names this as its premise-failure reading. It does not mention that g_iter1's trySpawn already routes respawners to a fresh carrier (Duck.java:172).
scores.graft: The objective branch in Micro.fight for committed ducks only: Chebyshev progress times a fixed weight, against a per-threat cost that does not depend on distance, in place of the engage, advance and kite branches. Strike-first and strike or heal after the move are kept. This fixes the rush formula's habit of overrunning threats at range, which every interception arm so far has inherited.

scores.name: Design 2: Situation Board: shared carrier tracks with claim-bounded interception
scores.strengths: Its numbers are the most rigorous. I reproduced every recomputed figure from trips-b2fs: 573 trips of 25+ rounds holding 298 captures; capture rates 74/49/31%; 132 long unopposed captured trips, 61% of them first grabs, 62% with at least one of our ducks within dist2 20 at the pickup (mean 2.35, within dist2 64 4.59, median start r462). It is the only design that brings out that the long unopposed walks are mostly first grabs, while chains dominate the short captures. The plan is information-first. S0a is a truth-only reachability test (icptPossible, with thresholds that route or close S1). S0b validates the sensor against replay truth through indicator dots (wmHit20, wmLat, wmDest, wmFalse), so a broken sensor cannot be mistaken for a wrong premise. Its bytecode table uses the real engine costs (I checked MethodCosts.txt: readSharedArray 2, writeSharedArray 75). 'Sym.observe exists but is never called' is true. S2 and S3 run only if their own premise numbers hold, and it predicts that S3 will fail. Its closing criteria include a band-level premise test: the enemyCaptured delta must be -2 SE or better to advance.
scores.weaknesses: The interceptor still fights through the unchanged rush path: fight(enemies, allies, goal) with taskThreat 150 and the d2*4 goal term, with engage and advance keeping priority. That is g1icpt's micro, so the stated difference is information only. It does not address the fact that ducks taking the 20000 carrier branch already chase a carrier they can see. Low chasers after a pickup they witnessed therefore points as much to chasers dying or being hurt (body count) as to forgetting. Eligibility includes engaged ducks, and displacement is allowed, which ADVICE warns causes churn. S2's premise is partly wrong: 'reinforcements walk to a static target' ignores that g_iter1's trySpawn already sends respawners to an alerted flag home (Duck.java:171-173) and that fieldTarget pulls ducks within ALERT_RADIUS2. S2 also sits close to the refuted family of more defenders and wider alerts (12-31). K is clamped at 3-5, below the 6.76 escort pack.
scores.graft: The S0a/S0b sequence: a truth-only premise test (icptPossible on kept replays) before any behaviour code, then a sensor-only build scored against replay truth (wmHit20, wmLat, wmDest via indicator dots), with a closing rule if the prediction cannot be had.

scores.name: Design 1: Task-claimed squads: HUNT / CONVOY / GUARD / RAID over a shared task table
scores.strengths: The premise arithmetic is explicit and correct. I reproduced 312 of 453 captures at 20+ rounds, the 71/47/33/24% rates by chaser bucket (n 192/224/120/135), 416 low-chaser long trips with 241 captures, savings of 55 to 141 captures (0.25 to 0.64 a game), and our carrier deaths at 29% within 3 rounds and 49% within 6. The best lever unique to this design is respawners as the main hunters, claiming before they spawn. Post-setup deaths run about 0.54 a round (294 over r200-749), and long unopposed trips are 61% first grabs that start on our spawn centres. So the bodies 'free to act' appear exactly where the trips start, which answers the 'everyone is always in a fight' finding. Ordinary ducks can claim only if not engaged. The hunt size scales with the escorts seen (3 + escSeen). The convoy re-grab requires convoy count ≥ enemies + 1, a direct lesson from b2rg. There are execution diagnostics (hStaffed, predErr, hContact) and an in-game conversion diagnostic: contacted long trips captured ≤35%, against 58%. The schema bit layouts fit (OC_POS 12 bits ≤ 3835; OC_AUX HP/143 fits 3 bits).
scores.weaknesses: There is no offline premise screen. S0 only back-fills baselines, so HUNT and CONVOY behaviour is built before reachability is known. HUNT uses the rush formula verbatim (-th*150 - d2(goal)*4), with engage at 10000 kept and no leash, so hunters crossing a fight both overrun threats at range and get pinned. CONVOY is a co-equal stage despite b2rg, b2rgc, g1esc, g1esc2 and g1escrg all showing that our carriers die within about 3 moves inside their spawn. GUARD is a cousin of the refuted bodies-at-the-flag family (9-25, 12-31, 16-29, 19-23; T9: weak bots guard more), and RAID is a cousin of the flank squad. Both are conditional and state a difference, but they widen the scope. The HUNT want table gives no behaviour for a DROPPED track, so the chain final legs (141 short captures, 97% non-first) are left to the conditional GUARD. The S3 accept bar deviates from the pre-registered REWRITE_EVAL rule (upper-tier enemyCaptured with net ≥ +1 SE, instead of the capture-difference delta with net ≥ -5), which breaks 'numbers not moved'. Station indices taken from the claim count can collide when two ducks join in the same round.
scores.graft: Respawner-first hunters: jailed ducks claim the hunt before spawning and pick the spawn tile that minimises their intercept time. Field ducks may claim only when not engaged (no enemy within dist2 10), and the hunt size scales with the escorts seen. This answers 'who is free to act' using bodies that are out of the fight anyway.

scores.name: Design 4: Tide: commander-timed mass waves
scores.strengths: Its hook points are exact: I checked Duck.java lines 45, 173, 208, 307, 359, 608 and Micro lines 45 and 153. Its upper-tier numbers roughly reproduce from census-g_iter1.csv: kills 298 vs 314, inEnemy250 11.3 vs 23.0, pickups 5.2 vs 22.9, captured 0.5 vs 2.5. The +30 kill bounty paid only when the attacker stands on enemy territory is real (RULES.md:41) and is a genuine evidence-based economy insight. The commander and accumulator census is exact, one round late. The S0 instruments (supShare, loneDeaths, trickleDeaths, sideKills400) are useful, and it gives a table of differences from closed directions.
scores.weaknesses: It aims at the wrong deficit. Fights against the tier above are at parity (in losses we even lead, 331 vs 294), and 106 of 151 losses are by capture, but the capture lever (S6 RECOVER, the tracking) is optional and outside the budget. Its core parts restate closed directions with a clock: MASS is a hold-line (0/7; the opponent walked into our half while we held), PUSH at margin 1 is the closed aggression knob (83/81 vs 84), the push for ground is drift (g1drift80: inEnemy250 +2.3 gone by r300, kills -62), the rally is cohesion (20-23, 4-18), and the lull crumbs are the crumb detour (not reproduced). The evidence says ground bought early does not hold. The P1 screen (hazInf/hazSup ≥ 2) is close to a tautology, since outnumbered ducks die more by definition, so it cannot show whether a commander can manufacture superiority that converts. D5 (trickle) is assumed, not measured. The per-duck bytecode is underestimated: about 10 accumulator read-modify-writes at about 77 each is about 750, not 300-500. MASS phases invite raids while their first pickup median is r268.
scores.graft: The trickle and concentration instruments (loneDeaths, trickleDeaths, supShare and its hazard buckets) as guardrail columns for any responder design. They would show whether hunters or escorts arrive alone and die, which is the likely failure mode against a 6.76-duck escort pack.

judgements.recommendation:
On evidence fit I rank the designs ODM (8.5), Situation Board (8.0), task-claimed squads (7.5), then Tide (3.0). Tide aims at fights, which are at parity against the tier above. The deficit that decides games is captures: 106 of 151 losses are by capture, and 47% of their captured trips are unopposed. Tide puts that deficit in an optional stage outside its budget, and its main parts repeat refuted directions: hold-line, the margin-1 aggression knob, drift and cohesion.

I recommend a synthesis built on ODM:

1. **Premise first, no bot code.** Take Situation Board's S0a and ODM's P1-P6 on the kept g_iter1 band replays (reach, reach while in a fight, prediction error, destination hit, conversion prior), with the thresholds written now.
2. **Sensor-only build.** Take Situation Board's S0b, scored against replay truth through indicator dots (wmHit20, wmLat, wmDest). This separates sensor failure from premise failure.
3. **Tracks.** Key tracks by flag so they survive drops. This is the only way to reach the chain final legs: I recomputed that 141 of the 453 captures last under 20 rounds and 97% of those are not first grabs.
4. **Responders.** Take the squads design's respawner-first hunters (claim before spawning) and its rule that a field duck may claim only when not engaged, with the hunt size scaled to the escorts seen. Use ODM's rendezvous so responders arrive together rather than one at a time.
5. **Micro.** Use ODM's objective branch instead of the rush formula. All three interception designs otherwise inherit g1icpt's goal term, which overruns threats at range and lets engage pin the responder.
6. **Measures.** Make the squads design's in-game conversion check ("contacted long trips captured ≤35%") a step 5(a) premise diagnostic, so delivery is not judged on chasers20 alone. Add Tide's loneDeaths and trickleDeaths as guardrail columns.

Defer the escort/convoy stage until ODM's P4 or Situation Board's convoyReach holds. Five arms already show our carriers die within about 3 moves inside their spawn. Drop GUARD and threat routing unless their own premise numbers hold: g_iter1's trySpawn already sends respawners to an alerted flag, and the bodies-at-the-flag family is refuted.

Keep the REWRITE_EVAL bars unchanged. The squads design's modified accept rule should not be adopted.

scores.name: Design 2: Situation Board (shared carrier tracks + claim-bounded interception)
scores.strengths: It is the most buildable of the four, and its risky parts are checked one at a time. (1) The bytecode budget uses the engine's real costs. I checked engine.jar MethodCosts: readSharedArray 2, writeSharedArray 75, setIndicatorDot 0. Its 600-700 typical and about 2.8k worst-case adds are believable against the ~15k peak. (2) It changes Micro less than any other design: one static (taskThreat) plus the existing fight(enemies, allies, goal) overload. Its snippet matches Micro.java:208 exactly (-th*RUSH_THREAT_COST + adj*10 - d2(goal)*4), and Micro.java:153 shows a non-null goal already bypasses MICRO_V2 and HOLD_DRIFT. (3) Identity at switch-off is the most carefully guarded. Every WM/Tasks entry catches its own exceptions, which matters because RobotPlayer only catches at the top level, so a stray GameActionException would drop the rest of g_iter1's turn. WM never calls G.rand and keeps a private WM_SYM, so Sym.cands is never touched (Sym.cands drives enemyCenters and nearTheirSpawn). The tick writes WM_TICK last, so if the tick throws, the next robot redoes it. (4) Freezing Q is right. Nav.moveTo calls reset() whenever the target changes (Nav.java:262), so a moving goal would wipe the bug-nav state every turn. (5) Its claims check out: Sym.observe has no callers (grep), and tools/lib.sh does not override bc.engine.show-indicators. The Round schema has indicatorDotIds/Locs/Rgbs, so beliefs can go into replays at zero bytecode with no 64-character limit. (6) The order of stages is the cheapest way to fail. S0a is tools only, on g_iter1 replays that tools/keep-replays.txt keeps. S0b is the sensor only, with accuracy bars against replay truth (wmHit20, wmLat, wmFalse), so a sensor failure shows up before any consumer is built. (7) Respawn handling is robust: a jailed claimant's ETA includes its remaining jail time, and the tick role passes to whoever finds WM_TICK stale.
scores.weaknesses: (1) It uses 39 of the 41 free slots (23-61; only 62-63 spare), so later stages have no headroom. The sector board (SEC_ACC/SEC_PUB/SEC_EN, 12 slots, about 200-300 bytecode per duck per turn plus a 75-bytecode increment) is built and paid for in S0b, though only the conditional S2 consumes it. (2) Claim liveness uses a 3-bit stamp, 'live if stamp is r&7 or (r-1)&7', and nothing clears dead entries. A claim abandoned without being zeroed (release, displacement, a forgotten path) comes back to life for 2 rounds in every 8, inflates live(t) and blocks real claims. The tick needs to zero stale entries, or every release path must write 0. (3) Twelve claim entries are tight: 3 tracks at K up to 5 is 15, and S3's convoy tasks share the same table. (4) Running the objective through the rush overload keeps the engage branch (10000) and the advance branch (5000). A claimant that sees an enemy in reach still fights locally and steps toward Q only on turns when its action is not ready. This is the same dilution g1icpt showed (intercepts fired constantly while chasers20 stayed flat), so execution risk sits inside S1 rather than only in the premise. (5) There are two sources of symmetry truth: interceptors aim with WM_SYM while Micro.nearTheirSpawn and carrierTarget use Sym, and the two can disagree. (6) SEC_EN's 3-bit window stamp ((round>>2)&7) aliases every 32 rounds.
scores.graft: The S0b stage: a sensor that changes no behaviour, with exception isolation and a tick that writes its marker last. It is scored against replay truth through indicator dots (0 bytecode, verified in the schema) before any consumer exists, which separates sensor failure from strategy failure at almost no risk.

scores.name: Design 3: Objective-Driven Micro (ODM): flag tracks, capped responder auction, objective branch in Micro.fight
scores.strengths: (1) It uses the fewest slots (23-44, 22 slots, leaving 19 free). The auction is double-buffered by round parity and cleared under an 11-bit round stamp, so unlike Design 2's 3-bit stamps it cannot alias. The idx-0-runs-first premise holds: RULES.md line 31 says execution order is fixed creation order, and idx is claimed in that order. (2) The objective branch sits under the carrier branch (20000) and the loose-flag branch (19000) and replaces engage/advance/kite only for committed ducks. That is the only hook among the four that reliably turns an in-fight duck toward a team goal, without the engage-branch dilution that sank g1icpt. With k=0, 'obj = goal==null && kind!=NONE' is false, so identity follows directly. (3) holdAct is correct engineering. Micro.java:159 strikes first and spends the action, and the post-move pickup at line 217 needs actReady. Without holding the action, an escort fighting next to a dropped flag could never re-grab it. Design 1 misses this. (4) It is careful about determinism: Obj.nearestDet, a deterministic hash for thinning, and a BotTest that checks rngState before and after. Its BotTest gap is real: the slot-range list in test/bot/BotTest.java omits OF_HOME 20-22. (5) The auction needs one read-modify-write per bidder (75 bytecode), with no central writer. There is a bytecode guard (keep the last goal when fewer than 7,000 remain), and the worst case of about 3.8k gives a peak around 19k, which is plausible. (6) It cross-checks the bot's @trk predictions against the offline --track replay simulation, and computes the S0 premise from replays it already has (234 kept g_iter1 band replays).
scores.weaknesses: (1) The auction is the most intricate logic in any of the designs: buckets, binomial thinning, a first-round bid-only rule, a T_rv rendezvous, and a 10-round cooldown. It is unit-testable, but hard to debug from replays, and commitment lags the live track by at least 2 rounds. (2) The CUT goal is recomputed every turn as the prediction advances. Nav.moveTo resets bug state on any change of target (Nav.java:262), so out-of-fight responders lose their wall-following every turn and may stall on maze maps. It needs Design 2's frozen Q. (3) There is no symmetry check. The destination comes from Sym.best(), which rests only on the r<=3 broadcast hints because Sym.observe is never called. P3 (destHit) would detect a wrong symmetry but not repair it. (4) There is no exception isolation for the new code paths. (5) The clearing cost is underestimated: roundStart clears 6 slots at 75 each, about 450 bytecode, not the stated 120 worst case. It falls on one light robot, so it is immaterial. (6) A committed duck that dies keeps its Obj.kind statics. On respawn it can resume as committed alongside its replacement, so k can be overshot by one unless plan() treats a fresh spawn as an exit. (7) Its budget, about 6 VM days, is the largest.
scores.graft: The objective branch in Micro.fight that replaces engage/advance/kite only for committed ducks, plus holdAct so an escort keeps its action for a pickup. This is the in-fight hook that actually moves a committed duck, and k=0 keeps identity trivially.

scores.name: Design 1: Task-claimed squads (HUNT / CONVOY / GUARD / RAID over a shared task table)
scores.strengths: (1) The claim format is clean and robust to jail. It packs a 4-bit stamp, a 6-bit cur and a 6-bit last into 16 bits; idx 0, which always runs first, normalises it each round, and members heartbeat it. Membership therefore decays one round after a death, with no aliasing and no explicit release writes. Jail releases the role, and the dead carrier writes DOWN from jail (RULES.md line 30: unspawned robots run code). (2) Sym.observeSpawn is a real fix for a measured blind spot. MapInfo.getSpawnZoneTeamObject exists and costs 2 bytecode (engine MethodCosts). It is gated by bit 1 because Sym.cands changes g_iter1 behaviour, and symOk is measured in S0. (3) It names the RNG trap correctly: G.nearest calls rand(2) on ties (G.java). (4) Its bytecode estimate is plausible: about 250 for beginTurn with ~25 reads, a ~1,050 one-robot normalisation, and about +2.2k worst case, so roughly 17.5k peak. (5) HUNT and CONVOY are separate bits, so they can be delivered independently from one source.
scores.weaknesses: (1) It has the largest code surface: six roles, about 520 new lines (Roles, Track, Raid), and Micro changes in four places (leash filter, three branch gates, and a role bonus inside bestTarget, which every duck's tryAttack shares). More code means more chances to break identity and slower diagnosis. (2) S1 bundles Track (heading, speed, escorts, destination), claims, respawn hunters, the H path, Micro HUNT mode, Sym.observeSpawn and the MISSING/presumed-captured logic into one arm. When it fails, e1-e3 narrow the cause, but many mechanisms remain under each one. (3) Hunters keep the engage branch, which is the same local-fight absorption seen in g1icpt. (4) The convoy re-grab reuses the existing post-move canPickupFlag at Micro.java:217, which needs actReady. The strike-first call at line 159 usually spends the action, so escorts in a fight seldom re-grab, and there is no hold-action as in Design 3. (5) interceptPoint is recomputed every 2 rounds and convoy stations move every turn, so both trigger Nav.reset. (6) Station index is taken from the claim count at join time, so churn produces duplicate stations. (7) The respawner's spawn-tile choice is not free: the spawning turn continues into a full fight turn, so a heavy intercept search there risks an overrun. (8) It takes 29 slots, with S4/S5 slots reserved up front. The plan runs 6 stages, up to 12 arms and about 4 VM days, the longest path to a band reading.
scores.graft: The claim-slot format: a stamp, cur and last packed in 16 bits, normalised by idx 0 each round and heartbeated by members. Team counts then decay one round after a death or jailing, with no release writes and no aliasing. Also Sym.observeSpawn, gated by its switch.

scores.name: Design 4: Tide (commander-timed mass waves)
scores.strengths: (1) A single writer gives a consistent shared state. idx 0 runs first among our robots every round, fixed creation order (RULES.md line 31), including while jailed, so every duck sees the same phase and rally within a round. A stale WV_TICK triggers failover. (2) Its line numbers are accurate: Duck.java 56 (fight), 62 (crumbs), 173 (trySpawn), 208 (setup gather), 307 (carryFlag), 359 (fieldTarget fallback), 608 (trap reserve check). (3) S1 only observes: the census and the commander publish and nothing acts. This yields an exact alive count one round late, and a commander that can be tested as a pure next() function (WaveTest). (4) Geometry is cheap per duck: one signum and one distance per tile in Micro.
scores.weaknesses: (1) It has the heaviest write load. Each army duck in contact does about 9-10 accumulator read-modify-writes at 75 bytecode each, about 750 in writes alone, against the stated 300-500 for Wave.report. idx 0 also clears about 13 accumulators every round. It still fits (about 16.5k peak), but the estimate is about 2x low for that component, and packing the counters would halve it. (2) The blast radius is the widest. S2 changes setup's gather point (feeding the load-bearing dam traps), the spawn target and the fieldTarget fallback for all 47 army ducks. S3 changes the advance margin and kite pull in Micro for all of them. When a stage fails, its several bundled sub-mechanisms are hard to tell apart. (3) It is the least robust to map variety. It relies on an axis from spawn centroids, a line-abreast formation about 12 tiles wide (slots can land in walls or water), and a rally clamped to 0.25-0.60 of the axis. On maze or tunnel maps that means congestion and unreachable slots. (4) The enemy centroid E comes from Sym, which has never been verified (Sym.observe is never called), and nothing checks it. A wrong symmetry misdirects wave 1 and the whole axis. (5) The estimators are approximate: trap kills are not counted in k25, respawn delays bias N_them_est, and about 20 tunable constants plus a phase machine add hysteresis and flapping risk. (6) It has no exception isolation for the commander beyond the stale-tick failover, and a commander exception that comes after the clear but before the publish loses a round of totals.
scores.graft: The S1 commander that only observes: idx-0 single-writer accumulators (alive, contact, kills, deaths) published one round late with failover. It is an exact team census any design can read, at a write cost of about 75 per counter.

judgements.recommendation:
On engineering feasibility, Design 2 ranks first, Design 3 second, Design 1 third and Design 4 fourth.

Build Design 2's stage order:
- S0a: the premise test from replay truth, tools only, on the kept g_iter1 replays.
- S0b: the sensor with no behaviour change, checked for identity and scored against replay truth through indicator dots.

Keep from Design 2:
- exception isolation on every new entry point;
- no G.rand anywhere in the new code;
- a private symmetry copy that never writes Sym.cands;
- WM_TICK written last;
- a frozen intercept point Q, because Nav.java:262 resets bug state on any change of target.

Change four things before coding:
1. **Claim table.** Replace it with Design 3's double-buffered auction, cleared each round under an 11-bit stamp. At minimum, have the tick zero claim entries whose 3-bit stamp is stale; today a dead claim comes back to life for 2 rounds in every 8.
2. **Micro hook.** Route the objective through Design 3's objective branch, which replaces engage/advance/kite only for committed ducks and holds the action for pickups. Do not use the rush-goal overload: it keeps the engage branch, which is how g1icpt's intercepts fired without moving chasers20.
3. **Symmetry.** Add Design 1's Sym.observeSpawn (MapInfo.getSpawnZoneTeamObject exists and costs 2 bytecode), gated by its switch, or let the private WM_SYM feed the destination.
4. **Sector board.** Defer it until S2's premise passes. That frees about 12 slots and about 250 bytecode per duck per turn.

Bytecode is not the binding constraint for any design. With writeSharedArray at 75 and reads at 2, every design stays at or below about 19k against a ~15k base. The real risks are identity breaks from uncaught exceptions or RNG use, Nav resets on moving goals, and in-fight hooks that never actually move ducks. Design 4's commander census is worth keeping as a neutral instrument, but its wave behaviour touches all 47 army ducks per stage and depends on geometry that breaks on maze maps.

scores.name: Design 2: Situation Board (shared carrier tracks + claim-bounded interception)
scores.strengths: This is the best-staged design for separating sensor failure from premise failure. S0a is a premise gate that needs no bot code. It runs on replays the VM already kept: g_iter1 is in tools/keep-replays.txt, and the band runs 20261001-011402 and -021054 have 120 games each. It has a pre-written kill switch (icptPossible < 0.25 closes the programme). S0b is the sensor alone, with behaviour identical to g_iter1. Its delivery checks (wmLat, wmHit20, wmFalse, wmDest, wmMiss) compare the bot's beliefs with replay truth, so they are low-noise and test execution directly. The fire condition depends on an event happening: mean:icptMiss<=0.1 counts only trips of 10+ rounds. A plain unconditional fire share would fail with perfect execution: on the B3 band only 207 of 232 games have one of their trips of 10+ rounds. The behaviour change is small and bounded. It uses the existing Micro.fight(enemies, allies, goal) overload (Micro.java:153) plus one static. Every field duck stays byte-for-byte g_iter1. There are at most 12 claim entries with K 3-5 per track. A try/catch on every entry point protects the identity check. A private WM_SYM keeps Sym.cands untouched; Sym.observe is never called in src/bot, which I verified. The premise is judged at the 234-game band test: enemyCaptured must be at -2 SE or better to advance and closes the programme above -1 SE. The paired SE there is about 0.08 against an expected -0.25, so that test has power. The cost figures hold up: writeSharedArray 75, readSharedArray 2 and setIndicatorDot 0 in the 3.0.6 MethodCosts; dots are recorded because show-indicators defaults to true (Config.java:66) and lib.sh does not override it. Of all four designs, its closing criteria end the programme earliest and cheapest when the premise is wrong.
scores.weaknesses:
1. Interceptors fight through the rush-micro goal branch (Micro.java:208: -th*150 - d2(goal)*4). Engage (:199) and advance (:201) keep priority, so a claimant with something in reach stays in the local fight. The goal term grows by 8d-4 per step, so beyond about 19 tiles it outweighs one threat. g1icpt failed on this same path, so the first arm may well fail on execution; icptReach would catch it, but it costs an arm.
2. The 5(a) games are g_iter1 mirrors. g_iter1 makes few long carrier trips, so there is little for the mechanism to fire on. REWRITE_EVAL's curriculum asks for archetype opponents (owner prompt 113).
3. The S0b delivery bundles board metrics (wmAllyErr, wmEnemyRecall), which only S2 needs, with the track metrics S1 needs. A board failure could block S1.
4. Acceptance needs +2 SE over 960 paired games. That replaces the pre-registered REWRITE_EVAL bars (a)/(b) plus confirmation; it is stricter, but the protocol is inconsistent.
5. Between -1 and -2 SE on enemyCaptured the band rule says nothing.
6. Dots need new ReplayDump parsing code. The replay already stores each team's shared array every round (GameMaker.java:612-617, 687), so TRK slots could be scored directly.
scores.graft: S0a plus S0b: a premise gate from replay truth before any bot code, then a sensor-only build with behaviour identical to g_iter1, whose delivery checks score the tracks against replay truth (latency, hit rate within dist2 20, false tracks, destination) before any consumer exists.

scores.name: Design 3: Objective-Driven Micro (tracks + capped responder auction + objective branch)
scores.strengths: It has the strongest pre-registration discipline. Weights, bars, premise thresholds and closing criteria are fixed before code ('never moved'). It adopts REWRITE_EVAL's bars (a)/(b), confirmation and regression guard as written. S0 runs in shadow mode with k=0 and identity. It adds an offline replay-dump --track premise census on the 234 kept g_iter1 band replays: P1 prediction error, P2 reach, P3 destination hit. It also checks in-bot predictions against the offline simulation. Its 5(a) opponents follow the curriculum: g1escrg (13-27 pickups per game in its own 5(a)) and arch_rush10. That gives the CUT mechanism far more enemy trips per diagnostic game than a mirror. The execution signatures are measurable: committed count within k+-2, and the responders' Chebyshev distance to the true carrier at the end of each unseen stretch. The objective score is scale-free (+-1 tile of progress x w, threat 250), which avoids the rush-micro problem it correctly diagnoses (d2 x 4 against 150). Two other claims are right. It says escorts recruited within ESCORT_R2 = 20 cannot raise escorts20, which is measured at that same radius. It says BotTest's range list omits OF_HOME 20..22 (BotTest.java:20). Running both doses as one attempt keeps the budget honest at 7 mini-blocks and 3 band runs.
scores.weaknesses:
1. P1 and P3 are computed offline with the TRUE enemy centres. The bot uses Sym.best(), which never prunes beyond the round-3 broadcast hints and defaults to rotation. The offline premise can therefore pass while in-bot prediction fails, and there is no symOk check.
2. P6 does not specify which trips it covers. On trips-b2fs.csv the ratio is 0.19 over all trips but 0.51 over trips of 25+ rounds, so the bar passes or fails depending on a choice made after seeing the data.
3. P4's first clause passes trivially (62% of our trips last 6+ rounds).
4. fire:objTurns>0>=0.9 counts all games. Only 89-94% of games have a qualifying enemy trip, so a perfect implementation fails the fire bar roughly 20-50% of the time.
5. C3 closes a stage after two failures of the kills>=0.92 or firstGrabs<=1.15 guards. At n=24 the paired kills SE is about 61 on a base of about 450 (scaled from b2rg's -37 at -1.9 SE), so the kills guard alone fails about 28% of the time under the null.
6. The objective branch replaces engage and advance for committed ducks, and the k=8 dose raises the fight cost if the premise is wrong.
7. The auction (bucket histograms, hash thinning, T_rv) is the most intricate mechanism of the four.
8. The @trk agreement check needs a driver game that keeps stdout; diag-batch.sh does not pass robot-player-to-system-out.
scores.graft: Run step 5(a) against our own archetype builds (g1escrg convoy chains, arch_rush10) rather than g_iter1 mirrors, so the mechanism has many enemy trips to act on. Pair this with the scale-free, Chebyshev-progress objective score that never outweighs threat cost at range.

scores.name: Design 1: Task-claimed squads (HUNT / CONVOY / GUARD / RAID)
scores.strengths: S0 is a proper identity stage: every census and survey value must equal the g1copy mirror, with max bytecode 18k or less. The census does not parse indicator strings, so the indicator re-layout is safe. S0 also back-fills baselines on the cached dg909090 base and measures symOk, the true symmetry against Sym's choice. That is the one design that checks the bot's own symmetry knowledge. The execution diagnostics map one to one onto sub-mechanisms: e1 staffing, e2 prediction error from a per-hunter 'p' indicator field against the true carrier, and e3 contact. HUNT and CONVOY are delivered separately on g_iter1, which keeps the readings clean. The design spots the G.nearest/G.rand trap (G.java:471-479) and uses a tie-free nearestDet. The APIs it relies on exist (MapInfo.getSpawnZoneTeamObject, rc.getGlobalUpgrades(Team)). The claim heartbeat (max(cur, last), normalised by idx 0, which always runs first per RULES) is sound. The trip statistics it cites are correct: 312 of 453 captured trips last 20+ rounds, with capture rates of 71/47/33/24% by chaser bucket.
scores.weaknesses:
1. Nothing tests the premise before code. No offline check asks whether free ducks can reach the path in time. The power claim (+13 to +22 net, +2 to +3.4 SE) treats observational chaser buckets as causal.
2. S1 bundles Track, claims, respawner hunters, the HUNT micro mode, MISSING detection and Sym.observeSpawn. Sym.observeSpawn changes Sym.cands for the whole army through Comms.syncSym, so S1's outcome mixes HUNT with better symmetry for the field.
3. The delivery block is overloaded. S1 has 5 rel: guards, some tight (enemyCaptured<=1.0, captured>=0.85). S2 has an outcome bar on 24 games (captured>=1.1). By my estimate a working arm passes about 20-30% of the time, so 'two delivery failures with e1-e3 passing = premise failure' would often close a working stage.
4. Its fire bars (0.85 and 0.8) sit below the mandatory 0.9 in TRAINING_ALGORITHM §3.5 (CLAUDE rule 13), instead of being made conditional on the event.
5. Its S3 acceptance bar (band +1 SE with upper-tier enemyCaptured -2 SE) differs from the pre-registered REWRITE_EVAL (b) (capture-difference delta with net >= -5).
6. It has the largest surface: 4 roles, 29 slots, invasive Micro edits (leash filter, branch gates, targeting bonus) and up to 0.4·A = 20 non-field ducks, so the fight-cost downside is the biggest of the three tracking designs.
7. Its 5(a) games are self-play mirrors.
8. The roughly 1k bytecode for idx 0's normalisation writes is left out of the estimate (harmless).
scores.graft: Execution diagnostics split by sub-mechanism (staffing share, prediction error read from a per-hunter predicted point, contact share), plus the S0 symOk check that compares Sym's chosen symmetry with the truth.

scores.name: Design 4: Tide (commander-timed mass waves)
scores.strengths: Its instruments are excellent and reusable: supShare/infShare, hazard by local-superiority bucket, loneDeaths, trickleDeaths, sideKills400, pushExch, and a --wave mode that scores the commander's estimates (N_us, N_them_est, k25) against replay truth. S1 is an observe-only commander with identity and accuracy checks. It also previews the 'virtual pushes' the commander would order during g_iter1's own play, which tests the decision logic for free. Every line reference I checked is accurate (Duck.java:17/173/208/359/608, Micro.java:45 and 153-220). It adopts REWRITE_EVAL's bars and pre-registers one second dose per stage. idx 0 running first every round is engine-confirmed (fixed creation order).
scores.weaknesses:
1. The S0 premise screen P1 (hazInf/hazSup >= 2) is close to a tautology, because outnumbered ducks die more by construction. It will pass and screens nothing. The real premise test (C3: upper-tier exchange by r600) comes only at M1, after S1-S3 are built.
2. It changes the behaviour of all 47 field ducks: fieldTarget fallback, spawn want, setup gather point, and fight margins and pulls. Those mechanisms are a composite of closed directions: cohesion (refuted), hold-line (0/7), drift (band 11-24, kills -62) and the global aggression margin. That gives the largest downside if the premise is wrong.
3. About 25 tunable constants (MASS_PCT, PUSH_EDGE, STRIKE_EDGE, ABORT_EDGE, PULL weights...) with one pre-registered dose per stage make a delivery failure hard to attribute to a parameter rather than the premise.
4. S4 re-times combat stun traps, the one trap habit that ablation found load-bearing (16-26).
5. The bytecode estimate for Wave.report is low: up to about 11 ACC writes at 75 each is about 825 before the enemy loop, against the claimed 300-500. It is still under the line.
6. The largest measured deficit (unopposed carriers) is left to an optional S6.
7. S1 is 'fixed until it passes, outside the budget', which is open-ended.
scores.graft: The --wave/S1 shadow-commander method: run the team decision logic with every action off, publish its state, and score both its estimates and the decisions it would have made against replay truth (virtual pushes during the incumbent's own games) before it controls anything.

judgements.recommendation:
Under the testability and risk lens, build Design 2's staging as the backbone. First, S0a: a premise gate computed from replay truth on the kept g_iter1 band replays, before any bot code. Then S0b: a sensor that leaves behaviour identical to g_iter1, delivered on low-noise belief-against-truth checks. Then S1: a bounded number of claimants, with the field army byte-for-byte g_iter1. If the premise is wrong, this design closes earliest and cheapest, and it changes the least of what already works.

Graft these onto it:

1. **Step 5(a) opponents (from Design 3).** Use the archetype builds g1escrg and arch_rush10 instead of g_iter1 mirrors, so the mechanism has many enemy trips to act on.

2. **Objective scoring (from Design 3).** Replace the rush-micro goal path with Design 3's scale-free score: +-1 tile of Chebyshev progress x w, with threat cost 250. In the current goal path (Micro.java:208), the d2 x 4 term outweighs the 150 threat cost beyond about 19 tiles. Engage and advance (Micro.java:199/201) also keep claimants in local fights, the same path g1icpt failed on.

3. **Symmetry and prediction checks (from Design 1).** Add S0's symOk check and the per-claimant prediction-error field. Neither design 2's nor design 3's offline premise uses the bot's own symmetry: Design 3 assumes the true enemy centres, and Design 2's private symmetry is unvalidated until S0b.

4. **Score beliefs from the stored shared array.** Every .bc24 already holds each team's shared array per round (GameMaker.java:612-617, 687; ReplayDump does not read it yet). Track and claim beliefs can be scored against truth on every delivery and band replay, without dots or stdout.

Fix the delivery checks in whichever design is chosen. As written they would misclassify working arms.

- **Fire bars.** Make them depend on the event happening, e.g. Design 2's mean:icptMiss, or Design 3's F x (share of base cells with the event). An unconditional fire share fails because only 89-94% of games have a qualifying enemy trip. Set the bar from the cached dg909090 base cells.
- **Outcome guards on 24 games.** At n=24 the paired SE is about 13% of base for kills and about 0.25 for enemyCaptured. Under the null, a kills>=0.9-0.92 guard fails 23-28% of the time, and five such guards cut a working arm's pass rate to about 20-30%. Keep only loose guards in delivery (roughly 1.5 SE: kills>=0.8, enemyCaptured<=1.25). Judge outcomes and premise at the 234-game band test against the pre-registered REWRITE_EVAL bars (a)/(b), plus confirmation. Do not use design-specific acceptance bars.
- **Specify premise bars exactly.** Design 3's P6 ratio is 0.19 over all trips but 0.51 over trips of 25+ rounds on trips-b2fs.csv. Pin down the subset of every premise bar before computing it.

Budgets: the VM-day estimates do not bind. A 120-game band seed takes about 14 minutes on the VM, so the arm and attempt caps are the real closing criteria. State them as such.

Do not adopt Tide for now. Its premise screen will pass whatever the truth, its real test comes three stages in, and it rewires every field duck through directions already closed. Its --wave shadow-commander instruments are worth keeping on their own.
